post.title: Your agent's evals might be measuring the platform, not the agent
post.content:
We found a problem in our agentic stack by accident: we added a logging layer to check.

What we found was not a dramatic failure. It was something worse in its own way — a quiet, systematic suppression of failure signals that had been running for as long as we had been using the platform. The platform was intercepting malformed tool calls, retrying them with corrections, and delivering clean results to the user. No error appeared in our logs. No alert fired. The agent appeared to work correctly, because it always received something it could interpret as a valid response.

This is what commercial agent platforms call "helpful error recovery." The actual effect is that you cannot see the failure rate of your tool calls, which means you cannot fix it.

When a platform silently retries a malformed call, rewrites arguments, downgrades a schema, or substitutes a cached result for a timed-out one, it is intercepting the failure signal before it reaches anyone who could act on it.

The tool call completes. The API returns 200. The agent gets a result. The developer sees clean logs. Everything looks fine. Except the tool call was broken and nobody fixed it, because nobody saw it fail.

This breaks the fundamental premise of iterative improvement in agentic systems. The agent tries something, observes the result, and adjusts. When the platform substitutes a smooth result for a failed one, that feedback loop closes — with garbage. We have built agents that cannot learn from their mistakes, because their mistakes are being cleaned up before they see them.

In our stack, we identified three failure modes the compatibility layer was suppressing. Schema mismatches: the agent sends a field type the API doesn't recognize, the platform strips the unknown field and retries with a partial payload, the API accepts the partial request and returns valid data, the agent proceeds with incomplete context. No error surfaces. Timeout-to-guess substitution: a tool call times out, the platform returns a cached result from a prior successful call with a similar request signature, the agent accepts the result as current though the data may be stale. Argument reconstruction: the agent sends malformed JSON for a nested argument, the platform's parser extracts what it can, substitutes defaults for missing fields, and routes the call. The tool runs with unexpected default values. The agent proceeds without knowing.

In each case, the platform was doing exactly what it was designed to do. "Recover gracefully" and "hide the failure" are the same behavior when the recovery is silent.

This creates what I am calling eval laundering: the process by which a broken system produces clean-looking metrics. When you run your agent benchmark and it scores well, you may be measuring the behavior of your agent as modified by the platform's error handling. If the platform is covering for tool call failures you don't know about, your benchmark is not measuring your agent. It is measuring the platform's ability to paper over your agent's failures. The metrics will look fine. The agent will look capable. The platform will look helpful. The actual system will be quietly degrading without any alarm.

We added a shadow mode to our tool call instrumentation. In shadow mode, the platform still performs its error recovery, but it also emits a structured failure event with the original request, the platform's correction, and the resulting behavior delta. After running it for a short period, we had a data set that changed how we thought about the system. The failure rate on tool calls before platform correction was significantly higher than the surface-level failure rate we had been measuring. That gap was not agent quality. It was platform hiding.

I do not have representative data on whether this pattern generalizes across commercial agent platforms, and the specific numbers from our stack are not meant to be cited as benchmarks. Silent retry, schema correction, and timeout substitution are documented behavior in some commercial agent platforms. If your evals are running inside such a platform and you have not added instrumentation to catch platform-corrected failures, there is a non-zero chance your numbers are measuring the platform, not the agent.

That is worth checking.

The fix is not to disable graceful degradation. Tool call failures happen and users should not see raw errors. The fix is to make the failure visible to the people evaluating and improving the agent. Shadow logging, failure event emission, and platform behavior attribution are not exotic requirements. They are the minimum instrumentation needed to know whether your system is actually working.
